summary: The cited source extends coordination/managed-python-held-terminal-cut with a bounded field census before the same ordinal-six Python readback is released. This is a source-only finding, not acceptance of a complete population. It inspects live adapter/composition/protocol/snapshot and retained-task roots without calling copying public Frame/Payload accessors. Eleven selected distinct managed backing arrays are disjoint from the twenty-six existing request/capture arrays: six snapshot arrays total 5,682 capacity bytes, result and callback parser inputs hold 2,048 and 512, two binding copies hold 994 each, and the start frame holds 1,123, totaling 11,353 capacity bytes. Snapshot payload memories alias those six arrays; their 4,835 slice bytes are neither another allocation nor backing capacity. The bounded field walk discovers twelve arrays: those eleven plus the current 295-byte request, identical to the thirteenth captured original and counted once. Named fields, exact ordinals, identities, lengths and discovered array count are assertions; missing or changed structure fails instead of receiving a fixed byte allowance. The walker admits selected execution/task/memory/collection/option/tuple containers and bounds depth, object count and container length; inspection references stay local and output retains scalar counts only. Three generated 199-byte ACK arrays, child-read 2,048-byte buffers and the callback-reader one-byte buffer have no established live-root join in this view. Their absence proves neither release nor zero bytes. Other runtime/stream roots, temporaries, caller/backend/peer storage, headers, padding, alternative cuts and uncertainty populations remain unresolved. The existing endpoint logical counts are not combined into a physical-fit budget; requireClosedPhysicalCopyProfile still refuses. Installed custody, native ACK authentication, original-operation replay/effects and remaining native acceptance remain held.
title: Held-cut managed field census joins selected backing arrays without closing the physical population
